newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-DSM ups payout despite lower earnings.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-DSM ups payout despite lower earnings.

text.p: Dutch petrochemicals group DSM NV reported a 32.7 percent drop in 1996 earnings on Tuesday but said it would raise its dividend in line with a new pay-out policy aimed at wooing long-term investors.
DSM said its 1996 net profit fell to 720 million guilders ($383 million) from 1.07 billion in 1995, due mainly to a margin squeeze in its bulk hydrocarbons and polymers activities.
Fourth quarter net profits fell to 129 million guilders from 144 million.
Finance director Louk Ligthart said full-year operating profits had fallen from the record levels of 1995 due to lower margins on most of DSM's products.

"Lower margins at polymers and fibre raw materials (caprolactam and acrylonitrile) resulted from lower sales price in combination with strongly higher raw material costs for polymers," Ligthart told a results news conference.
In addition, a longer-than-expected stop for maintenance at one of DSM's naphtha crackers had also undermined operating earnings, he said.
While sales prices had increased throughout 1996, overall they had lagged behind those of 1995, he said.
DSM chairman Simon de Bree said earnings for the first half of 1997 would be comparable to those in the same period of 1996.

"In the markets that are important to DSM demand continues to develop favourably. As far as can be judged at present, margins, in particular those for polymers, will gradually improve," he said, reiterating an earlier statement.
"Based on this, DSM expects that the results for the first half of 1997 will reach a level comparable to that of the first half of 1996."
Despite the lower results, DSM said it was raising its dividend to nine guilders from the eight guilders of a year ago, reflecting an amendment to its dividend policy.
"From 1996 the dividend will be determined as a percentage of the cash flow from ordinary operations after deduction of the fixed dividend to holders of cumulative preference shares," Ligthart said.
The percentage cashflow would lie between 16-20 percent, he added. DSM paid a 1996 preference dividend of 28 million guilders, but this is set to rise to 35 million guilders in the years 1997-2005.
"This (dividend move) would make our stock more attractive to stay in (investors') portfolios...we want to create a more solid, stable shareholders' base," Ligthart said.
The move was aimed at creating a more predictable pay-out and if price-earnings ratios of the stock increased as a result this would be a bonus, Ligthart added.
From 1996 onwards DSM would also offer pay-outs in shares, buying back shares in the market for this purpose to prevent dilution of per-share earnings, Ligthart said.
DSM could also opt to buy back more shares if equity levels rose to such an extent they undermined the targeted 15 percent return on equity, he added.

Analysts welcomed Tuesday's results, saying that while overall earnings were in line with an indicative figure issued by DSM in January, the core hydrocarbons and polymers business did better than expected.

"The figures were above expectations, notably due to a better than expected performance of the hydrocarbons/polymers division. The rise in oil prices did not pressure results as much as expected," Peter Schouten of MeesPierson said.
Nils van Elzelingen of NIBStrating said prior to the results he had expected slightly lower profits in 1997 but that he had now revised this to a slight increase.
"Earnings from hydrocarbons and polymers were above my expectations...That will have a positive follow-through effect in 1997," he said. ($ = 1.882 Dutch Guilders)
